questions.chapter: Public Key Cryptography and Hash Functions
questions.text: Explain Digital Signatures and Public Key Infrastructure (PKI). Describe how digital signatures provide authentication, integrity, and non-repudiation. Explain X.509 Digital Certificates, Certificate Authorities (CAs), and Certificate Revocation Lists (CRLs).

Compare Block Cipher Modes of Operation: Electronic Codebook (ECB), Cipher Block Chaining (CBC), Cipher Feedback (CFB), Output Feedback (OFB), and Counter (CTR) mode with respect to initialization vectors (IV), error propagation, and security.

Explain the Advanced Encryption Standard (AES). Describe the internal state matrix ($4 \times 4$), key expansion algorithm, and the four round transformations: SubBytes, ShiftRows, MixColumns, and AddRoundKey.
questions.solutionOutline: Symmetric block cipher (128-bit block, keys: 128/192/256 bits with 10/12/14 rounds). State organized as 4x4 byte matrix. SubBytes: non-linear byte substitution using S-box over GF(2^8). ShiftRows: cyclical left shift of rows 0, 1, 2, 3 by 0, 1, 2, 3 bytes. MixColumns: matrix multiplication over GF(2^8) diffusing bits across columns. AddRoundKey: XOR with round subkey. MixColumns omitted in final round.

questions.text: Compare Block Cipher Modes of Operation: Electronic Codebook (ECB), Cipher Block Chaining (CBC), Cipher Feedback (CFB), Output Feedback (OFB), and Counter (CTR) mode with IV initialization and error propagation characteristics.
questions.solutionOutline: ECB: encrypts identical plaintext blocks to identical ciphertext (leaks pattern, insecure). CBC: XORs plaintext with previous ciphertext block using IV (serial encryption, parallel decryption, self-synchronizing). OFB: keystream generated by feedback of encrypted IV; stream cipher mode, no error propagation. CTR: encrypts IV+counter; enables full parallel encryption and decryption and random access.

questions.text: Explain the Diffie-Hellman Key Exchange algorithm. Formulate the mathematical computation over multiplicative group $\mathbb{Z}_p^*$, and explain how the Man-in-the-Middle (MITM) attack compromises unauthenticated Diffie-Hellman.
questions.solutionOutline: Public prime p and generator g. Alice chooses private a, sends A = g^a mod p. Bob chooses private b, sends B = g^b mod p. Shared secret K = B^a mod p = A^b mod p = g^(ab) mod p. Discrete logarithm problem makes computing a from A hard. MITM: active attacker intercepts A and B, establishes separate keys K1 with Alice and K2 with Bob. Prevented by digital signatures / PKI certificates.

questions.chapter: Public Key Cryptography and Hash Functions
questions.text: Explain Cryptographic Hash Functions: SHA-256 and MD5. Describe Merkle-Damgård construction, collision resistance, pre-image resistance, and second pre-image resistance.
questions.solutionOutline: One-way compression mapping arbitrary message to fixed-size digest (256 bits). Properties: 1) Pre-image resistance (given h, hard to find m such that H(m)=h); 2) Second pre-image resistance (given m1, hard to find m2 != m1 with H(m1)=H(m2)); 3) Collision resistance (hard to find any pair m1 != m2 with H(m1)=H(m2)). Merkle-Damgard pads message, splits into 512-bit blocks, and applies iterative compression function.

questions.text: Explain HMAC (Hash-based Message Authentication Code). Derive the formulation $\text{HMAC}(K, m) = H((K \oplus opad) \parallel H((K \oplus ipad) \parallel m))$ and explain why it prevents length extension attacks.
questions.solutionOutline: Message authentication using shared secret K and cryptographic hash function H. Pads key to block size. ipad = 0x36, opad = 0x5c. Inner hash computes H((K xor ipad) || m); outer hash hashes padded key with inner hash output. Nested double-hash structure prevents length-extension attacks that affect naive H(K || m) constructions.

questions.text: Describe the Kerberos Protocol (Version 5). Detail the message exchanges between Client, Authentication Server (AS), Ticket Granting Server (TGS), and Target Application Server using Ticket Granting Tickets (TGT).
questions.solutionOutline: Trusted third-party authentication protocol. 1) Client requests TGT from AS; AS verifies client and returns TGT encrypted with TGS secret key plus client-TGS session key. 2) Client sends TGT and Authenticator to TGS requesting Service Ticket. 3) TGS decrypts TGT, validates authenticator, and issues Service Ticket encrypted with server key. 4) Client presents Service Ticket to Server for mutual authentication.

questions.chapter: Network Layer and Transport Layer Security
questions.text: Explain the Transport Layer Security (TLS 1.3) Handshake Protocol. How does TLS 1.3 achieve 1-RTT connection establishment, forward secrecy via ephemeral Diffie-Hellman (ECDHE), and 0-RTT resumption?
questions.solutionOutline: TLS 1.3 deprecates legacy ciphers (RSA key exchange, CBC modes). 1-RTT handshake: ClientHello sends supported cipher suites and ECDHE key share simultaneously; ServerHello responds with chosen cipher and server key share, deriving master key immediately. Mandatory ECDHE guarantees Forward Secrecy. 0-RTT early data allows client to send encrypted data on first flight using pre-shared resumption key.

questions.text: Describe Firewalls and their classifications: Packet Filtering Firewalls (Stateless), Stateful Inspection Firewalls, Application Layer Gateways (Proxy Firewalls), and Next-Generation Firewalls (NGFW).
questions.solutionOutline: Firewalls enforce access control policies at network boundary. Packet filter: inspects IP headers (src/dst IP, port, protocol) independently (Layer 3/4). Stateful inspection: tracks TCP connection state (SYN, ESTABLISHED), dynamically permitting return traffic. Proxy firewall: terminates client connection and creates separate server connection at Layer 7. NGFW: integrates deep packet inspection (DPI), application awareness, and TLS decryption.

questions.text: Explain Intrusion Detection and Prevention Systems (IDS/IPS). Compare Signature-Based (Misuse) Detection with Anomaly-Based Detection. Differentiate between Network IDS (NIDS) and Host IDS (HIDS).
questions.solutionOutline: IDS detects unauthorized activity; IPS actively blocks offending traffic inline. Signature-based: matches traffic against known attack patterns (high accuracy for known exploits, blind to zero-days). Anomaly-based: establishes baseline statistical profile of normal network behavior and flags statistical deviations (detects novel attacks, high false-positive rate). NIDS monitors promiscuous tap; HIDS monitors system calls on individual host.

questions.text: Explain Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS) attacks: SYN Flood, UDP Amplification, and DNS Amplification. Describe DDoS mitigation strategies (SYN cookies, Rate Limiting, Anycast BGP routing, Scrubbing centers).
questions.solutionOutline: DDoS exhausts network bandwidth or server compute resources via distributed botnets. SYN Flood fills half-open TCP backlog queue; mitigated by SYN cookies (encoding connection state in initial sequence number without allocating kernel memory). Amplification abuses open UDP/DNS resolvers sending small requests with spoofed victim IP, reflecting massive payloads. Mitigated by BGP Anycast distributing attack volume.

questions.chapter: Public Key Cryptography and Hash Functions
questions.text: Explain X.509 Public Key Infrastructure (PKI) digital certificates: certificate fields, hierarchical trust chains (Root CA, Intermediate CA), Certificate Revocation Lists (CRL), and Online Certificate Status Protocol (OCSP).
questions.solutionOutline: Binds public key to entity identity signed by Certificate Authority. X.509 fields: Version, Serial Number, Issuer, Validity Period, Subject, Public Key Info, Signature Algorithm, Extensions (SAN). Validation traces signature up to trusted Root CA in browser trust store. Revocation checked via CRL (downloaded signed list of revoked serials) or OCSP (real-time query/OCSP stapling).

questions.chapter: Public Key Cryptography and Hash Functions
questions.text: Explain Elliptic Curve Cryptography (ECC). Formulate the Weierstrass equation $y^2 = x^3 + ax + b \pmod p$, point addition, and point doubling operations. Why does ECC offer equivalent security to RSA with significantly smaller key sizes?
questions.solutionOutline: Based on algebraic structure of elliptic curves over finite fields GF(p). Group law defines point addition P + Q = R by drawing chord intersecting curve and reflecting across x-axis; point doubling 2P uses tangent line. Security relies on Elliptic Curve Discrete Logarithm Problem (ECDLP) which requires fully exponential Pollard-rho solving time, enabling 256-bit ECC keys to match 3072-bit RSA security.

questions.chapter: Network Layer and Transport Layer Security
questions.text: Explain Wireless LAN Security: WEP, WPA, WPA2, and WPA3. Discuss WEP's RC4 IV reuse vulnerability and explain the 4-Way Handshake in WPA2-PSK and SAE (Simultaneous Authentication of Equals) in WPA3.
questions.solutionOutline: WEP: 24-bit IV with RC4 keystream reuse allows recovery of WEP key within minutes (Fluhrer-Mantin-Shamir attack). WPA introduced TKIP with per-packet key mixing. WPA2 uses robust AES-CCMP encryption; 4-Way Handshake derives Pairwise Transient Key (PTK) from PMK/passphrase. WPA3 replaces PSK with SAE (Dragonfly handshake), preventing offline dictionary attacks and providing forward secrecy.

questions.text: Explain Buffer Overflow vulnerabilities in C/C++. Provide the mechanism of stack-based buffer overflow (overwriting instruction pointer EIP on stack frame) and defensive mitigations: ASLR, Stack Canaries, and DEP/NX.
questions.solutionOutline: Occurs when data written to memory buffer exceeds allocated boundary without bounds checking (e.g. strcpy, gets). Stack frame layout: Local variables -> Saved Frame Pointer (EBP) -> Return Address (EIP). Attacker overflows buffer, overwrites return address with shellcode address. Defenses: Stack Canaries (random value before return address checked at epilogue), ASLR (randomizes stack/heap base addresses), DEP/NX (marks stack non-executable).
